name: Wei Jingsheng
milestone_by_age_26: Fame arrived at age 28 with 'The Fifth Modernization' essay posted on Democracy Wall in December 1978; no material milestone by age 26 found. He was working as an electrician at Beijing Zoo from 1973 to 1978.
early_history_summary: Wei joined the Red Guards at 16 during the Cultural Revolution and served in the People's Liberation Army from 1969 to 1973 before becoming an electrician at the Beijing Zoo. His political awakening came from witnessing rural poverty during the Cultural Revolution, but he did not publicly voice dissent until the Democracy Wall movement in 1978.
family_context_summary: Born to Chinese Communist Party cadres; raised in the Party school system with exposure to Beijing party elite internal dynamics.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were longtime Chinese Communist Party cadres; no direct activism or intellectual domain transfer documented.
evidence_summary: Wei Jingsheng's defining achievement—the Democracy Wall essay 'The Fifth Modernization'—occurred in December 1978 when he was 28, well beyond the age-26 cutoff. Before that, he was an electrician at the Beijing Zoo with no public dissident activity. His parents were Communist Party cadres, but this did not translate into early activism.

name: On Kawara
milestone_by_age_26: Major conceptual art works (Today date-painting series) began in 1966 at age 33; early Tokyo avant-garde paintings from 1955-56 are recognized only retrospectively in museum collections, with no specific dated milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Kawara moved to Tokyo in 1951 after graduating high school and became active in the city's postwar avant-garde art community. He was self-taught and produced violently satirical paintings in the early 1950s, but his defining conceptual work emerged only after he settled in New York in 1965.
family_context_summary: Born in Kariya, Japan to an intellectual family environment informed by Buddhist, Shinto, and Christian religion. His father was director of an engineering company, which enabled Kawara's move to Mexico in 1959.
parent_family_domain_summary: Raised in an intellectual family with religious influences; father was an engineering company director. No direct art-world family background documented.
evidence_summary: Kawara was active in Tokyo's postwar avant-garde by the early 1950s and produced notable paintings in 1955-56, but these works were only recognized retrospectively in museum collections. His defining conceptual art practice (the Today series) began in 1966 at age 33, well beyond the age-26 cutoff. No specific dated material milestone by 26 was found.

name: Oleg Protopopov
milestone_by_age_26: Won Soviet Championship medals in pairs skating from 1953 onward and debuted at European and World Championships by 1958, establishing himself as a nationally competitive skater by age 26.
early_history_summary: Protopopov started skating relatively late at age 15 and was coached by Nina Lepninskaya. He was drafted into the Baltic Fleet in 1951 but used leave time to skate, winning his first Soviet Championship medal in 1953 with partner Margarita Bogoyavlenskaya before meeting Ludmila Belousova in 1954 and forming a legendary partnership.
family_context_summary: Raised by his mother, a professional ballet dancer, and his stepfather, a poet, in Leningrad; his father abandoned the family when he was six months old. He survived the Siege of Leningrad as a child, eating wood glue for survival.
parent_family_domain_summary: His mother was a professional ballet dancer whose artistic sensibility later informed his lyrical skating style; his stepfather was a poet. No direct skating background in the family.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet sports system, ballet dancer mother, Siege of Leningrad survival, skating partnership with Belousova
evidence_summary: Protopopov started skating at 15, relatively late, and survived the Siege of Leningrad as a child with his ballet dancer mother and poet stepfather. He won Soviet Championship medals from 1953 and formed a legendary partnership with Ludmila Belousova, whom he married in 1957. The Soviet sports system provided institutional support through clubs like VSS Lokomotiv and access to elite coaches. His mother's ballet background informed the artistic quality that later revolutionized pairs skating.
starting_point: Born in Leningrad to a ballet dancer mother and poet stepfather; father abandoned the family when he was six months old; survived the Siege of Leningrad as a child.
current_position: Died in October 2023 at age 91 in Interlaken, Switzerland; two-time Olympic champion and four-time World champion in pairs figure skating who defected to Switzerland in 1979.

trajectory.event: Won Soviet Championship medal in pairs skating with first partner Margarita Bogoyavlenskaya.
Won Soviet Championship silver with Ludmila Belousova and married her in December.
Debuted at European Championships (10th) and World Championships (13th) with Belousova.
Won first World Championship medal (silver), becoming the first Soviet pair to win a world medal.
Won Olympic gold medal at Innsbruck, becoming the first Soviet pair to win Olympic gold.
Won second Olympic gold at Grenoble and completed four consecutive World and European Championship titles.
Defected to Switzerland while on tour, later obtaining Swiss citizenship in 1995.
Died on October 31 in Interlaken, Switzerland.

name: Simona Păucă
milestone_by_age_26: Won two Olympic gold medals (balance beam and team) and an all-around bronze at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics at age 14.
early_history_summary: Păucă began gymnastics at age 5-7 at a sports school in Bucharest under coach Iulia Rotarascu, then transferred to Dinamo București in 1982 under coaches Emilia Lita and Florin Stefanescu. She was a surprising medalist at the 1984 Olympics, which was her first and last major international competition.
family_context_summary: Born in Azuga, Romania; family background not well documented. Her father had a conflict with coaches at the Deva training center in 1985, which led to her suspension from international competitions.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Romanian gymnastics pipeline, early specialization, elite coaching from age 5, Olympic gold at 14
evidence_summary: Păucă began gymnastics training around age 5-7 in Bucharest under coach Iulia Rotarascu and transferred to Dinamo București in 1982. The Romanian gymnastics system, one of the world's strongest at the time, provided elite coaching and facilities that enabled her to win two Olympic gold medals at age 14. Her family background is not well documented, though her father's later conflict with coaches cut her international career short. She was a product of the intense Romanian gymnastics pipeline rather than family-domain advantage.
starting_point: Born in Azuga, Romania; family background not well documented; began gymnastics at age 5-7 in Bucharest.
current_position: Retired gymnastics coach living in Romania; two-time Olympic gold medalist (1984) who transitioned to youth coaching after retiring from competition in 1986.

trajectory.event: Began gymnastics at CSS nr. 2 Bucharest under coach Iulia Rotarascu.
Transferred to Dinamo București under coaches Emilia Lita and Florin Stefanescu.
Won two Olympic gold medals (balance beam and team) and all-around bronze at the Los Angeles Olympics.
Suspended from international competitions for a year due to her father's conflict with coaches at Deva.
Retired from competitive gymnastics and began studying to become a coach.
Began working as a youth gymnastics coach at CSS nr. 7 Dinamo București.

name: Ambiga Sreenevasan
milestone_by_age_26: Called to the English Bar in 1980 (age 24) and the Malaysian Bar in 1982 (age 26); these are standard professional qualifications, not exceptional achievements. Her major human rights work and Bar Council presidency came after age 50.
early_history_summary: Ambiga read law at Exeter University, graduating in 1979, and was called to the English Bar at Gray's Inn in 1980 before being admitted as an advocate and solicitor of the High Court of Malaya in 1982. She then worked as a legal assistant at Skrine before becoming a partner in 1991.
family_context_summary: Born in Seremban to Datuk Dr Gopal Ayer Sreenevasan, a pioneering Malaysian surgeon regarded as the father of urology in Malaysia, and Datin Visalakshi Subramaniam, who held degrees in Sanskrit and Economics from Indian universities.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a pioneering surgeon and mother was university-educated; professional and academic family background but not directly in law.
evidence_summary: Ambiga was called to the English Bar at 24 and the Malaysian Bar at 26, which are standard professional qualifications rather than exceptional achievements. Her defining work—Bar Council presidency (2007), Bersih 2.0 leadership, and major judicial reform—came decades later. She came from an elite family (father a pioneering surgeon) and attended Exeter University, but no material milestone by 26 was found.

name: Geoffrey Hinton
milestone_by_age_26: Was a PhD student at the University of Edinburgh at age 26; his PhD was awarded in 1978 at age 31. The backpropagation paper was published in 1986 at age 39, and the Turing Award came in 2018.
early_history_summary: Hinton graduated with a BA in experimental psychology from Cambridge in 1970, spent a year as a carpentry apprentice, then began PhD studies in artificial intelligence at Edinburgh in 1972. His doctoral work on neural networks was supervised by Christopher Longuet-Higgins and completed in 1978.
family_context_summary: Born in Wimbledon, UK into a family of distinguished scientists; father Howard Everest Hinton was a noted entomologist, and he is the great-great-grandson of mathematician George Boole and Mary Everest Boole. His mother told him 'Be an academic, or be a failure.'
parent_family_domain_summary: Deep intellectual lineage: great-great-grandfather George Boole founded Boolean logic, great-grandfather Charles Howard Hinton was a mathematician, father was a distinguished entomologist. Multiple family members in science and mathematics.
evidence_summary: Hinton came from an extraordinary scientific lineage including George Boole and multiple mathematicians, and his father was a noted entomologist. However, at age 26 he was simply a PhD student at Edinburgh with no material published achievement. His groundbreaking work on backpropagation came at 39, the Turing Award at 71, and the Nobel Prize at 77. No material milestone by 26 was found.

name: Fabrice Jeannet
milestone_by_age_26: Won World Junior title in 2000, World Championship bronze medals (individual and team) in 2001, World Championship individual gold in 2003, and Olympic team gold in 2004—all by age 24.
early_history_summary: Jeannet started fencing at age 4.5 in Martinique following his parents who both practiced the sport at regional level. He trained at INSEP (French national sports institute) and rose rapidly through junior and senior ranks, winning the World Junior title at 19 and World Championship bronze at 20.
family_context_summary: Born in Fort-de-France, Martinique to parents Gilles and Roseline, who both practiced fencing at regional level. His older brother Jérôme (four years older) also became an elite fencer and Olympic teammate. His mother passed away in 2000.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents practiced fencing at regional level, providing direct domain immersion from age 4.5. His brother Jérôme became a fellow Olympic champion fencer, creating a family fencing dynasty.
primary_early_advantage_tags: fencing family, early start at 4.5, INSEP, sibling partnership with Jérôme, French fencing tradition
evidence_summary: Jeannet began fencing at age 4.5 in Martinique, immersed in the sport through both parents who fenced at regional level. His brother Jérôme, four years older, became his Olympic teammate and lifelong training partner. The INSEP national sports institute provided elite training, and the French fencing tradition gave him a competitive ecosystem. By 20 he had World Championship medals, by 22 he was individual World Champion, and by 23 he had Olympic gold. The family fencing immersion was the dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Fort-de-France, Martinique to parents who both practiced fencing at regional level; started fencing at age 4.5 following family tradition.
current_position: Retired from competitive fencing after the 2008 Olympics; pursued a career in IT; two-time Olympic team gold medalist and individual World champion.

trajectory.event: Started fencing in Fort-de-France, Martinique, following his parents who both practiced the sport at regional level.
Won World Junior title, establishing himself among the world's best young fencers.
Won bronze medals (individual and team) at the World Championships in Nîmes.
Won individual World Championship gold in Havana, beating Maksym Khvorost in the final.
Won Olympic team gold at the Athens Olympics with his brother Jérôme and teammates.
Won Olympic team gold and individual silver at the Beijing Olympics, then retired to pursue an IT career.

name: Kentaro Miura
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 34th Newcomer Manga Award from Weekly Shōnen Magazine in 1985 at age 19, and began serialization of Berserk in 1989 at age 23, which became one of the best-selling manga series of all time.
early_history_summary: Miura created his first manga at age 10 and developed professional drawing techniques by middle school. He attended an artistic curriculum in high school, where he met fellow future mangaka Kouji Mori, and won the Newcomer Manga Award at 19 while applying to Nihon University's art college. At 18, manga artist George Morikawa acknowledged his skill was already professional and dismissed him as an assistant.
family_context_summary: Born in Chiba, Japan to parents who were both artists—his father made storyboards for television commercials and his mother taught art. The family moved frequently during his childhood, and drawing became his way of making new friends.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were working artists: father in commercial storyboards, mother as an art teacher. This provided direct domain immersion in visual arts from birth and normalized artistic production as a daily activity.
primary_early_advantage_tags: artist parents, early manga creation at 10, doujinshi community, art college, professional-level skills by 18
evidence_summary: Miura was born to two artist parents—father a commercial storyboard artist, mother an art teacher—giving him immersive domain exposure from birth. He created his first manga at 10, used professional techniques by 13, and was acknowledged as already professional-level by established mangaka George Morikawa at 18. He won the Newcomer Manga Award at 19 and launched Berserk at 23, which sold over 60 million copies. The family art background and Japan's manga ecosystem were the dominant early advantages, supplemented by the doujinshi community and art school peers.
starting_point: Born in Chiba, Japan to artist parents—father made storyboards for commercials, mother taught art; family moved frequently during childhood.
current_position: Died on May 6, 2021 at age 54 from acute aortic dissection; creator of Berserk, one of the best-selling manga series of all time with over 60 million copies in circulation.

trajectory.event: Created his first manga Miuranger, published in a school publication, spanning 40 volumes.
Won the 34th Newcomer Manga Award from Weekly Shōnen Magazine for Futatabi, gaining admission to Nihon University's art college.
Published the Berserk Prototype in Monthly ComiComi, winning a Manga School competition prize.
Began serialization of Berserk in Monthly Animal House, which would become his life's work.
Received the Award for Excellence at the sixth Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize for Berserk.
Died on May 6 from acute aortic dissection; Berserk had over 60 million copies in circulation.

name: Rudi Dutschke
milestone_by_age_26: Became a leading figure in the SDS by 1965-66 at age 24-25, but his defining moments—the 1968 student protests and assassination attempt—occurred at age 28. No specific dated material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Dutschke fled East Germany to West Berlin in October 1960, just before the Berlin Wall was built, after being refused university education for his political views. He studied sociology at the Free University of Berlin and joined the SDS in early 1965, quickly becoming its most prominent leader.
family_context_summary: Born in Schönefeld near Luckenwalde, Brandenburg, the fourth son of a postal clerk. Raised in East Germany with a Christian upbringing, he joined the Free German Youth in 1956 aiming at a sporting career as a decathlete.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a postal clerk; no political or intellectual family background documented. Working-class East German family.
evidence_summary: Dutschke joined the SDS in early 1965 at age 24-25 and quickly became a prominent leader, but his defining achievements—the 1967-68 protest actions, the Easter 1968 unrest, and the April 1968 assassination attempt—all occurred at age 28. While he was a rising figure by 26, no specific dated material milestone by that age was found. He came from a working-class East German family and was refused university education there for his political views.

name: Branislav Pokrajac
milestone_by_age_26: Debuted for the Yugoslav national team at age 18 in December 1965, won World Championship bronze at 23 in 1970, and Olympic gold at 25 in 1972—all by age 26.
early_history_summary: Pokrajac started playing handball as a student at the Fifth Belgrade Gymnasium and was a multi-sport athlete from youth, becoming a Yugoslav pioneer champion in partisan all-around at 12 and running 100m in 11 seconds at 17. He debuted for the national team at 18 and was considered the best left winger in the world during the 1970s.
family_context_summary: Born in Belgrade; father Stevan was an active footballer who hoped his son would follow in his footsteps, while mother Angelina preferred he focus on academics. He was a multi-sport athlete from youth, excelling in football, volleyball, athletics, and handball.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an active footballer, providing a sports-oriented family environment, but Pokrajac was drawn to handball rather than football. The family had athletic background but not specifically in handball.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Yugoslav sports system, multi-sport athlete, father footballer, early national team debut at 18, Red Star Belgrade
evidence_summary: Pokrajac was a multi-sport athlete from youth in Belgrade, becoming a Yugoslav pioneer champion at 12 and excelling in athletics by 17. His father was an active footballer, but Pokrajac chose handball and debuted for the national team at 18. The Yugoslav sports system, including clubs like Crvena zvezda (Red Star Belgrade), provided the institutional pipeline. He won Olympic gold at 25 and was considered the best left winger in the world during the 1970s. Family background was sports-oriented but modest, with his mother preferring academic pursuits.
starting_point: Born in Belgrade, Yugoslavia; father was an active footballer, mother preferred academics; multi-sport athlete from young age.
current_position: Died on April 5, 2018 at age 71 in Belgrade; Olympic gold medalist (1972), renowned handball coach who led Yugoslavia to Olympic gold in 1984, and professor of handball at the Faculty of Physical Education.

trajectory.event: Debuted for the Yugoslav national team in December, scoring his first international goal against West Germany in Belgrade.
Won World Championship bronze in France, signaling Yugoslavia's emergence as a handball power.
Won Olympic gold medal at the Munich Olympics, the crowning achievement of his playing career.
Won World Championship bronze in East Germany, his second world medal.
Played his final national team game at the Montreal Olympics, retiring with 180 caps and 510 international goals.
Led Yugoslavia to Olympic gold as head coach at the Los Angeles Olympics.
Died on April 5 in Belgrade, Serbia.

name: Arnaldo Cézar Coelho
milestone_by_age_26: Became a FIFA-listed referee in 1968 at age 25, which is a professional accreditation rather than a major achievement. His defining achievement—officiating the 1982 World Cup final—came at age 39.
early_history_summary: Coelho began as a beach soccer referee in Rio de Janeiro and became professional in 1965. He was appointed to the FIFA international list in 1968 and was selected for the 1978 and 1982 World Cups, becoming the first non-European to referee a World Cup final in 1982.
family_context_summary: Born in Rio de Janeiro; father was a pharmaceutical salesman for American companies in Brazil, mother was a postal worker. His brother Ronaldo Cezar Coelho became a founder of the PSDB political party in Brazil.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a pharmaceutical salesman and mother was a postal worker; middle-class family. No direct sports or refereeing background in the family.
evidence_summary: Coelho became a FIFA-listed referee in 1968 at age 25, which is a professional accreditation rather than a material achievement milestone. His defining accomplishment—officiating the 1982 FIFA World Cup final as the first non-European to do so—came at age 39. He came from a middle-class Rio family (father a pharmaceutical salesman, mother a postal worker) and studied physical education before specializing in refereeing.

name: Tigran Mansurian
milestone_by_age_26: Was a postgraduate student at the Yerevan Komitas State Conservatory at age 26; his first major recognition—the All-Union competition first prize in Moscow—came in 1966 at age 27.
early_history_summary: Mansurian moved from Beirut to Soviet Armenia in 1947 and settled in Yerevan in 1956. He studied at the Romanos Melikian Music School under Edvard Baghdasaryan from 1956-60, then at the Yerevan Komitas State Conservatory from 1960-65, followed by postgraduate studies from 1965-67. He began teaching at the Conservatory in 1967.
family_context_summary: Born in Beirut, Lebanon to Armenian parents; family moved to Soviet Armenia in 1947 and settled in Yerevan in 1956. His early childhood was affected by the Armenian Genocide's shadow on his family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Armenian family displaced by the Genocide; no direct musical family background documented. Mansurian was largely self-taught in solfeggio and music notation before formal training.
evidence_summary: Mansurian was a postgraduate student at the Yerevan Conservatory at age 26, having studied composition since 1956. His first major recognition—the All-Union competition first prize in Moscow—came in 1966 at age 27, just past the cutoff. He was born to Armenian parents in Beirut, moved to Soviet Armenia as a child, and was largely self-taught in music before formal training. No material milestone by 26 was found.
